title: From Solid-State Spin Defects to Fluorescent Proteins: A Perspective on Quantum Optical Sensing Platforms for Biomedical Applications
authors: Jyotiprakash Parhi, Ayan Majumder, Kasturi Saha
abstract: Quantum optical sensing has evolved from isolated solid state spin defect platforms to increasingly bio-integrated systems designed for biomedical applications. This review presents a perspective on this transition, spanning nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond to emerging fluorescent protein based spin qubits. Advances in diamond fabrication have enabled photonic cavities, nanomechanical resonators, and microstructured devices that enhance spin photon interactions and room temperature sensitivity. Exploration of spin defects in alternative materials further expands the sensing landscape. Parallel progress toward biological compatibility includes chip based architectures for in vitro and in vivo studies, microfluidic integration, and minimally invasive nanodiamond probes capable of intracellular nanothermometry and nanorheometry. Improvements in surface functionalization have enhanced coherence and sensing reliability in complex environments. Collectively, these advances highlight the progress and remaining challenges toward application oriented quantum sensing for the life sciences.
summary: This review surveys the field of quantum optical sensing, detailing the shift from solid-state quantum emitters like NV centers to bio-integrated systems using fluorescent proteins. It highlights the advanced techniques used to measure physical parameters like temperature and magnetic fields at the nanoscale. The paper emphasizes that while progress is rapid, overcoming environmental noise and ensuring scalability remain key challenges for clinical translation.
main_problem: The paper reviews the evolution of quantum optical sensing platforms, tracking the transition from isolated solid-state spin defects to bio-integrated systems for biomedical applications.
main_result: Significant progress has been made in integrating quantum sensors, utilizing platforms like NV centers, SiV centers, and fluorescent proteins, for nanoscale measurements in complex biological environments.
method: The review synthesizes various experimental techniques, including Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR), T1 relaxometry, and specialized readout methods like OADF, applied across different physical systems.
model_or_system: The core systems discussed are solid-state spin defects (e.g., NV centers in diamond, $	ext{V}_{	ext{B}}^-$ in hBN) and engineered biological systems (fluorescent proteins). These platforms are used to probe local fields like temperature, strain, and magnetic fields.
key_observables: Temperature, strain, electric fields, magnetic fields, longitudinal relaxation time ($T_1$), and spin-photon interactions.
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, nanometer-scale resolution, and coherence time in aqueous environments.
main_assumptions: The primary challenge is maintaining quantum coherence and reliable sensing functionality when moving from controlled solid-state environments to complex, noisy biological media.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the various optically accessible spin defects (NV to hBN) and their diverse applications, ranging from radical detection to nanoscale NMR.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a perspective review, first establishing the historical progression of quantum sensing platforms, detailing the physics and advances in solid-state defects, then covering the integration into bio-compatible systems, and finally summarizing current challenges and future outlook.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges quantum optics and condensed matter physics into a tangible application domain (biomedicine), requiring deep knowledge of open quantum systems, decoherence mechanisms, and solid-state defect physics.
